q: What do I need to set up a proper reptile habitat?
What kind of heating and lighting do reptiles need?
What is the difference between UVA and UVB lighting for reptiles?
How do I maintain proper humidity for a reptile?
What substrate is best for reptile enclosures?
What are the basic requirements for reptile-keeping?
How do I choose the right enclosure for a reptile?
a: Reptile husbandry requires precise environmental control matching the species' natural habitat. Heating needs a thermal gradient (warm side and cool side) provided by overhead heat sources (ceramic heat emitters, halogen bulbs, deep heat projectors) or under-tank heaters regulated by a thermostat—never use heat rocks, which cause severe burns. UVB lighting is essential for diurnal species (bearded dragons, tegus, many lizards, turtles, tortoises) to synthesize vitamin D3 and metabolize calcium—without it they develop metabolic bone disease (MBD), a painful, crippling condition. UVB bulbs should be linear fluorescent (tube style) rather than compact coils, placed at the correct distance (varies by brand) and replaced every 6-12 months as UVB output declines even if visible light remains. Humidity requirements vary dramatically: tropical species (chameleons, crested geckos, green tree pythons) need 60-80% humidity maintained with misting systems, foggers, or hand misting, while desert species (leopard geckos, bearded dragons) need 20-40%. Substrate choices include bioactive soil mixes (best for tropical, planted setups), paper towels (quarantine and sick animals), reptile carpet (easy to clean but harbors bacteria), and species-specific options (sand mixed with soil for desert species, cypress mulch for high-humidity species). Never use calcium sand or walnut shell products—they cause fatal impaction if ingested.

q: What are good beginner snakes?
How do I care for a corn snake or ball python?
What do snakes eat and how often?
How do I handle a pet snake?
What size enclosure does a snake need?
What are common health problems in pet snakes?
How do I set up a snake tank?
a: Excellent beginner snakes include corn snakes (docile, 4-6 feet, easy feeders), ball pythons (gentle, manageable 3-5 feet, somewhat picky eaters), and king/milk snakes (hardy, colorful, good feeders). All snakes are strictly carnivorous: feed frozen-thawed rodents (pre-killed, never live—live prey can severely injure or kill the snake) appropriately sized (about 1-1.5 times the snake's widest body diameter). Hatchlings eat every 5-7 days, adults every 10-14 days. Enclosures should be secure (snakes are escape artists) with appropriate size (at least as long as the snake's body length for the longest dimension), a thermal gradient of 75-80°F cool side and 85-92°F warm side with a basking spot, two or more hide boxes (one on each end), a water dish large enough to soak in, and appropriate substrate (aspen for low-humidity species, cypress/soil mix for high-humidity). Shedding issues (retained eye caps, incomplete sheds) indicate humidity problems—provide a humid hide with damp sphagnum moss during shedding. Common health issues include respiratory infections (wheezing, bubbles at nose—often from low temperatures or humidity), mouth rot (infectious stomatitis), mites (tiny black dots moving on the snake), and inclusion body disease (IBD, incurable, seen in boas and pythons). Handle snakes gently, supporting their body fully, and do not handle 24-48 hours after feeding to prevent regurgitation.

q: How do I care for a bearded dragon?
What are good beginner lizards?
How do I care for a leopard gecko or crested gecko?
What do lizards eat?
How do I set up a lizard habitat?
What is metabolic bone disease in reptiles?
How do I care for a pet turtle or tortoise?
What is the difference between aquatic turtles and tortoises?
How long do turtles and tortoises live?
a: Bearded dragons are popular desert lizards requiring a 75+ gallon tank for adults, intense UVB and heat (basking spot 100-105°F, cool side 75-80°F), a varied omnivorous diet (80% insects: dubia roaches, crickets, black soldier fly larvae—and 20% vegetables: collard greens, mustard greens, squash, bell peppers), and calcium + D3 supplementation at most feedings. Leopard geckos are nocturnal (no UVB needed, but low-level UVB is beneficial) with a warm spot of 88-92°F, eat primarily insects, and need humid hides for shedding. Crested geckos are tropical, do best at room temperature (72-78°F, no additional heat needed), eat powdered meal replacement (Crested Gecko Diet) supplemented with insects. Metabolic bone disease (MBD) is the most common reptile health problem—caused by improper UVB, calcium deficiency, or imbalanced calcium-to-phosphorus ratio—resulting in soft, deformed bones, tremors, paralysis, and death. Turtles and tortoises need much larger enclosures (ponds or large indoor tubs for aquatic species, 4x8 foot minimum for small tortoises), specialized UVB and heat, and species-appropriate diets (aquatic turtles: protein-heavy when young, more herbivorous as adults; tortoises: high-fiber plant diet, never animal protein). Aquatic turtles need powerful filtration, basking platforms, and water heaters. Lifespan considerations are major: red-eared sliders live 25-35 years, Mediterranean tortoises 50-80+ years, and sulcata tortoises 70+ years reaching 100-200 pounds. Many common turtles (especially red-eared sliders) are illegal to sell in some regions due to invasive species concerns.

q: How do I care for pet frogs or amphibians?
What do amphibians need for housing?
What do pet frogs eat?
Are amphibians good pets for beginners?
How do I handle pet amphibians?
What is chytrid fungus in amphibians?
How do I set up a vivarium for dart frogs?
What do salamanders and newts need?
a: Amphibians require careful attention to water quality and skin sensitivity—their permeable skin absorbs everything in the environment, making them highly sensitive to toxins, chemicals, and improper handling. Never handle amphibians with dry hands or lotion-coated skin—use powder-free nitrile gloves rinsed with dechlorinated water. Popular beginner amphibians include White's tree frogs (hardy, tolerate some handling), tiger salamanders, and fire-bellied toads. Dart frogs (poison dart frogs) are advanced but popular for bioactive planted vivariums. Housing requirements: most amphibians need a humid, planted terrarium (70-90% humidity for tropical species) with a water feature for semi-aquatic species, plenty of hiding spots, and temperatures appropriate to species (tropical: 72-80°F; temperate: 60-75°F). All amphibians need dechlorinated or spring water—tap water chlorine/chloramines are lethal. Diet consists of live insects (fruit flies for small frogs, crickets, roaches, black soldier fly larvae, waxworms as treats) dusted with calcium and vitamin supplements. Chytridiomycosis (chytrid fungus) is a devastating infectious disease causing population declines worldwide—quarantine new amphibians, maintain clean conditions, and source from reputable captive breeders. Many salamanders and newts have specific temperature requirements (many temperate species need cool 55-68°F and cannot tolerate high temperatures). Axolotls are fully aquatic salamanders needing cool water (60-65°F), a cycled aquarium with low flow, soft substrate or bare bottom (to prevent impaction), and a protein-rich diet of earthworms and pellets—they are illegal in some regions (California, New Jersey) due to environmental concerns.
